page.title: What this model can and cannot tell you
page.intro: Butterfly City starts from real open data for 41 districts of Taipei and New Taipei, 2015 to 2025. What happens after you change a policy is simulated with a simple model. This page lists where the model is simplified, where data is missing and what we assumed instead, so that you can judge the results yourself.
page.disclosure: Initial data and events come from real open data. Policy outcomes are simulated, not predicted.
page.sourcesLink: Every number, source and method is listed in data/SOURCES.md in the project repository.

items.title: A simulation, not a forecast
items.text: If you change nothing, every number equals real history. When you change a policy, the model estimates the difference from history. It cannot say what would really have happened; it shows what follows from the assumptions listed here.

items.title: Ranges come from disagreeing studies
items.text: Some parameters have no single accepted value. The model runs with the lowest, middle and highest values found in studies and shows the range of results. The range is not a statistical confidence interval, and the real outcome could lie outside it.

items.title: Events are shown, not added
items.text: Real events such as interest rate changes, COVID-19 or credit controls are already in the real data. The model never adds their effect a second time. It also does not model how an event would change the effect of your policies.

items.title: Only five policy tools
items.text: The game covers five housing and commuting tools. Many other forces that shape rents and commutes, such as interest rates, wages, construction by private developers and jobs moving between districts, follow real history and cannot be changed.

items.title: Two tools are not yet in the model
items.text: Sublease and rental management and the holding tax are shown with their real history, but changing them has no effect in this version. They are marked 'Coming soon'.

items.title: Effect of social housing on nearby rents
items.text: The study used measured home prices near new subsidised housing in the United States, within about 0.1 mile of each project. The model assumes rents move like prices and spreads the effect over the whole district. Evidence for Taiwan is limited.

items.title: Social housing cost and construction time
items.text: The cost per home comes from three Taipei projects. The construction time is the median time from start to completion in the national social housing records. Real projects vary widely in both.

items.title: Rent subsidy and other tenants
items.text: Part of a rent subsidy may end up as higher rent. The model applies this only to households that receive the subsidy. A possible effect on the rents of other tenants is not modelled.

items.title: Average subsidy per household
items.text: Only one year of the average subsidy per household was published, so that average is used for every quarter.

items.title: No administration costs
items.text: Each dollar of rent subsidy or commuter pass subsidy is counted as one dollar of budget. Administration costs are not included because no sourced figure was found.

items.title: Commuter pass sales
items.text: Monthly pass sales were not published as a full series. The number of passes is estimated from one published sales figure, so pass-related budget figures are approximate.

items.title: Only registered leases
items.text: Rents come from leases registered in the government actual price registration system. Many leases are not registered, so the data may not represent every renter.

items.title: Districts with few rental records
items.text: Three rural districts had no rental records. Their rents are estimated from a nearby reference district, for example Pinglin from Xindian. These values are marked as estimated.

items.title: Small homes
items.text: Rent is calculated from the district median rent per square metre. Small studios usually cost more per square metre, so the rent burden of people in small homes, including some of the citizens you can follow, may be underestimated.

items.title: Household income is estimated
items.text: District income combines tax records with the national household survey. Tax records leave out transfer income such as pensions and benefits. The latest observed tax year is 2023; 2024 and 2025 are extrapolated. The tax series changes method between 2018 and 2019, and values are not compared across that break.

items.title: Income distribution
items.text: To count people above the rent line, the model assumes incomes in each district follow a log-normal distribution with the spread seen in tax data, and that renters have the same income distribution as all households.

items.title: Price-to-income ratio by district
items.text: The district ratio is the median sale price divided by estimated household income. It is an estimate made for this game, not an official statistic.

items.title: One rail network for all years
items.text: Commute times come from the rail network at the end of 2025 and are used for every quarter. Before lines opened between 2018 and 2023, real trips in some districts were longer than shown.

items.title: Estimated, not measured, trips
items.text: Each district is represented by its population-weighted centre, computed from village populations. A trip is the trip to the nearest station (walking, or by road when that is faster, for people who live far from a station), the rail time, transfers, and the trip from the station at the other end; or a road trip, whichever is shorter. Distances are straight lines multiplied by a detour factor from a United States study. Buses are not modelled as a separate mode.

items.title: Lines not included
items.text: The Taoyuan Airport MRT and the Sanying Line are not in the network. Linkou has no station in the model: its residents reach the network by road at Huilong station on the Zhonghe-Xinlu Line, about 7.6 km from the centre of Linkou, and for some destinations the road alone is faster. Because road speed is an assumption, Linkou commute times may be too long. The Danhai LRT is also left out; it lies entirely within Tamsui and affects only trips inside that district.

items.title: Walking speed, road speed and waiting time
items.text: Walking speed and the detour factor come from foreign studies. Road speed for Taipei comes from a published traffic index and is assumed to be the same in New Taipei, where suburban roads are often faster. Waiting time is half the morning peak interval between trains; the Wenhu Line had no timetable data and uses the median of the other lines.

items.title: Where jobs are
items.text: The number of jobs in each district comes from the 2021 Industry and Service Census, which does not count government offices, schools or the military. Districts with many public employers, such as Zhongzheng, have more jobs than shown.

items.title: Who works where
items.text: The 2020 census tells where residents work only as same district, other district in the same city, or another city. The model spreads the last two groups over districts by number of jobs, and counts everyone working outside Taipei and New Taipei as working in the other city. People who commute to Taoyuan or Keelung therefore appear to have shorter trips, and the number of long commutes may be too low.

items.title: Check against a survey
items.text: The modelled average trip from New Taipei to Taipei is {commuteModelled} minutes. A Ministry of Transportation and Communications survey reported about {commuteSurvey} minutes. The model was not adjusted to match it.

items.title: Moving choices are assumed
items.text: No data on moves between districts of Taipei and New Taipei was found. How strongly rent, commute time and commuting cost affect where people move is an assumption, marked as a gap in the sources.

items.title: Commuter pass and moving
items.text: The cost of commuting uses the Taipei Metro fare per minute. Fares stop rising at the maximum fare, so long trips may be given too high a cost. The commuter pass check against real data covers MRT trips only, not moves.

items.title: Where the lines are drawn
items.text: A resident counts as at risk above 30% of income spent on rent and as a ghost above 50%, the cost-burden lines used by housing agencies in the United States. For commutes, 45 minutes comes from a Taiwan survey of what commuters accept; 60 minutes is a line set by this project, with no study behind it. Other lines would give other counts.

items.title: Which homes the district count uses
items.text: The district ghost count compares household income with the median rent of a whole home, the kind of lease a household rents. People renting studios or rooms pay less but often earn less, and their burden may differ. Before 2023 the lease records do not say whether a home is whole or a room, so some rooms may be included.

items.title: People with both problems
items.text: Data on people with both a high rent burden and a long commute does not exist. The model assumes the two are independent when it removes double counting.

items.title: One ghost, many people
items.text: In the district panel, each ghost stands for 1,000 people; this is a display scale. Policies change these counts by tens to a few hundred people, so the figures above the districts show the change from real history instead: each ghost is about 10 more people above a line, and each butterfly about 10 fewer. The exact ghost count is always shown in the district panel.

items.title: Illustrative households
items.text: The six citizens are invented households, not real people. Their numbers are calculated from the district results at a chosen point of the income distribution, so they move with your policies, but a real household in the same district could be very different.

items.title: Simplifications
items.text: Each citizen has one commute, even in households where two people work. The model does not decide whether an individual citizen moves away; moving is calculated for districts as a whole.

items.title: No change means real history
items.text: Automated tests check that the model returns real history exactly when no policy is changed, for many generated inputs.

items.title: Check against a real policy change
items.text: The commuter pass part of the model was compared with the real change in Taipei Metro entries after TPASS started in July 2023, with tolerances fixed before the result was computed. Result: {backtestResult} Only Taipei Metro stations with data in every month of 2019 and 2023 are compared; New Taipei Metro lines have no station data. The first half of 2023 was still a recovery period after COVID-19, so part of the change may come from the recovery and not from the pass. The other tools could not be checked this way.

items.title: Low-use housing
items.text: The map can show the share of homes with very low electricity use, an indicator of empty homes, for the periods in which it was published. No policy in this version changes it.

backtestResult.notes: Filled from the computed values in docs/BACKTEST.md (main result). ratio is simulated central divided by observed. Pick one sentence per check.

direction.met: The modelled change went in the same direction as the real change.
direction.notMet: The modelled change went in the opposite direction to the real change.

ratio.met: The modelled change was {ratio} times the real change, inside the range of {toleranceLow} to {toleranceHigh} set in advance.
ratio.notMet: The modelled change was {ratio} times the real change, outside the range of {toleranceLow} to {toleranceHigh} set in advance.

range.met: The real change lies within the range of model results.
range.notMet: The real change lies outside the range of model results.
